Senses.Explanation: (乾) dry + (屎) shit + (橛) a short stub/stake: "a dry shit-stick" — the (廁籌), the wood or bamboo stick used to wipe in a latrine before paper (or a stick of dried dung). Attested uses in the corpus: Linji, having presented "the true person of no rank" (無位真人), strikes the questioner and says (無位真人是甚麼乾屎橛), then returns to his quarters; Yunmen answers "What is Buddha?" (如何是佛) with (乾屎橛) (Wumenguan 21), and answers "What is Śākyamuni's body?" (如何是釋迦身) the same way in his own Extended Record; Deshan Xuanjian (德山宣鑒) says (釋迦老子是乾屎橛)。(文殊普賢是擔屎漢); and it occurs as the idiom "what dry shit-stick are you hunting for here?" (覓什麼乾屎橛). The texts assign the word no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One term, one meaning, deployed in two distinct cases by different masters — do not cross-attribute them: (1) Linji's dismissal of (無位真人) with (乾屎橛) (五燈會元, 古尊宿語錄, and raised-case retellings); (2) Yunmen's answer to (如何是佛) (五燈會元, 禪宗頌古聯珠通集, and Yunmen's own 廣錄, the 釋迦身 variant). The paired sayings ‘Yunmen’s dry shit-stick’ (雲門乾屎橛) and ‘Dongshan’s three catties of hemp’ (洞山麻三斤) recurs across the record (e.g. B25n0145, J37nB396). Cross-ref (無位真人).

Occurrences.Kwic: 無位真人是甚麼乾屎橛。巖頭不覺吐舌。雪峯曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (定上座) (Dingshangzuo, a Linji heir) section — NOT the Linji section: Ding travels south, meets Yantou/Xuefeng/Qinshan, and raises (師遂舉臨濟上堂曰…) Linji's own case. The line is Linji's (濟拓開曰 無位真人是甚麼乾屎橛); Yantou (巖頭) sticks out his tongue and Xuefeng (雪峯) comments. A raised/retold case, not Linji's own record — so MasterName null per the raised-case rule, though the case is Linji's. X-canon lb ed=X 0227a10 (co-located ed=R138 0399b13 not used).

Raised/retold case, so MasterName null per the raised-case rule, though the case is Linji's. Independent witness of the case.
(雲門匡真禪師廣錄); the dismissive idiom — "what dry shit-stick are you hunting here to chew on?" (覓什麼乾屎橛咬). Yunmen's own record.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雲門匡真禪師廣錄) (Yunmen's own Extended Record); the (釋迦身) (Śākyamuni's body) variant of the same move — a primary-source witness.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘Baizhang's wild fox,’ the fixed label for a public case. In the received account an old man says that, when formerly teaching on Baizhang's mountain, he answered ‘does a person of great cultivation fall under cause and effect?’ with ‘does not fall under cause and effect’ (不落因果) and consequently passed five hundred lives as a wild fox. Baizhang answers the repeated question ‘is not blind to cause and effect’ (不昧因果); the old man reports release and asks for a monk's funeral. The case does not end with those paired phrases: Huangbo asks whether someone who never answered wrongly would still be a fox; Baizhang calls him forward and Huangbo slaps him, while Guishan later answers a question about the case by shaking a door panel. Later masters repeatedly raise it in the chamber, interrogate why one wording brings descent and the other release, and dispute the easy contrast: two monks argue that ‘not blind’ may not free the fox and ‘does not fall’ need not cause descent. Thus a fox narrative becomes a named, repeatedly reopened public case whose stable documentary parts are the old man's question, the paired answers, the funeral, and later testing; this entry does not adjudicate cause and effect beyond those recorded claims.
Senses.Note: 226 exact-headword hits in 96 allowlist texts; ‘wild fox’ (野狐) has 1,721 hits in 261 texts. The title is one case, not a second sense for the animal called a wild fox. Cross-checked the complete family: ‘does not fall under cause and effect’ (不落因果), ‘is not blind to cause and effect’ (不昧因果), the old man's release and funeral, Huangbo's slap, Guishan's door-panel response, later chamber questioning, and dissent over the usual fall/release pairing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baizhang answers the repeated question ‘is not blind to cause and effect’; the old man reports awakening and release immediately afterward.

Occurrences.Kwic: 時溈山在會下作典座。司馬頭陀舉野狐話問典座。作麼生。座撼門扇三下。

AlternateTargets: the top of a hundred-foot pole
at the tip of a hundred-foot pole
Senses.Explanation: Literally 'the top (頭) of a hundred-foot (百尺) pole (竿)': 623 hits / 196 allowlist files. The locus classicus is a verse in Changsha Jingcen's record (the 五燈會元, Compendium of the Five Lamps, under the head 湖南長沙景岑招賢禪師, 'Chan Master Jingcen Zhaoxian of Changsha, Hunan'; earliest witness the 祖堂集, Patriarchs' Hall Collection): (百尺竿頭不動人)。(雖然得入未為真)。(百尺竿頭須進步)。(十方世界是全身) — 'the person unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole, though he has gained entry, is not yet real; atop the hundred-foot pole he must step forward — the ten directions are the whole body.' The contrast (得入) ('gained entry') / (未為真) ('not yet real') is the verse's own words. From the verse comes a fixed question, (百尺竿頭如何進步) ('atop the hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?'; 88 hits / 58 files counting an optional intervening punctuation mark): asked of Changsha by Sansheng (承師有言『百尺竿頭須進步』 — 'I have it that you, master, said: atop the hundred-foot pole one must step forward' — Changsha's recorded answer: 朗州山，澧州水, 'the mountains of Langzhou, the waters of Lizhou', B25n0144); asked of Fadeng by a monk (僧問法燈百尺竿頭如何進步燈云噁, 'a monk asked Fadeng: atop the hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward? Deng said: E!', C077n1710 — the answer is the single syllable 噁); asked of Nanquan (泉云。更進一步, 'Quan said: step further', T47n1996), whereupon the same monk asks Waguan, who answers with a counter-question — (百尺竿頭用進作什麼)。(僧不肯)。(官便打) ('atop the hundred-foot pole, what would you step for?' The monk did not accept it; Waguan struck him. T47n1996; the master is 鹽官, Yanguan, in the X78n1556 telling). A master also puts the question to the assembly (石霜示眾云百尺竿頭如何進步, 'Shishuang addressed the assembly: atop the hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?', C078n1720), and Wumen fixes it as Case 46 (竿頭進步, 'stepping forward from the pole-top'), framing the question as Master Shishuang's (石霜和尚) and the verse as an unnamed old worthy's (古德). It is also given to be looked at: the story of Yu, the mountain-abbot of Chaling (茶陵郁山主), has him set the Fadeng exchange to look at (教令看, 'had him look at it', C078n1720), examining it in detail every day (由是每日叅詳, 'from then on he investigated it in detail daily', C077n1710; 凡三年, 'for three years in all', C078n1720) until he falls from a donkey crossing a bridge and (忽然大悟) ('suddenly greatly awakened'; C077n1710, C078n1720, D48n8939). First-line variants: (不動人) ('the unmoving person'; 8 hits / 8 files) vs (坐底人) ('the person sitting there'; 29 / 26).
Senses.Note: Attribution has a genuine framing spread (not a dispute over the reading). The VERSE (百尺竿頭不動人…須進步…十方世界是全身 — 'the person unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole… must step forward… the ten directions are the whole body') is Changsha Jingcen's in the lamp records — the (五燈會元) (Compendium of the Five Lamps) files it under his head, and comment-lines call its author (老長沙) ('Old Changsha', C078n1720). But the case-form circulated attached to others: Wumenguan Case 46 frames the QUESTION (百尺竿頭如何進步) ('atop the hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?') as Master Shishuang's (石霜和尚) and the verse as an unnamed old worthy's (古德); the (石霜示眾) ('Shishuang addressed the assembly') framing recurs (C078n1720). The corpus writes only '(石霜)' without disambiguating Shishuang Qingzhu (807–888) from Shishuang Chuyuan/Ciming (987–1040, per master-dates.json), so those lines are left MasterName null. In the classic exchange (三聖) (Sansheng Huiran) questions the verse's author: (承師有言)『(百尺竿頭須進步)』…(百尺竿頭如何進步) ('I have it that you, master, said: atop the hundred-foot pole one must step forward… atop the hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?', B25n0144). Textual variant of the verse's first line: (不動人) ('the unmoving person', 五燈會元) vs (坐底人) ('the person sitting there', 無門關, Wumen's Barrier). Related fixed phrases attested in the allowlist (counted over the 462-file allowlist, XML tags/notes/rdg stripped and line-break whitespace collapsed): (百尺竿頭) itself (623 hits / 196 files), (百尺竿頭進步) ('stepping forward from atop the hundred-foot pole', 53 hits / 41 files), (百尺竿頭如何進步) ('atop the hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?', 72 / 51 exact; 88 / 58 allowing one intervening punctuation mark), (竿頭進步) ('stepping forward from the pole-top', 113 / 81), (更進一步) ('step further', 81 / 60), (十方世界是全身) ('the ten directions are the whole body', 15 / 15), (百尺竿頭坐底人) ('the person sitting atop the hundred-foot pole', 29 / 26), (百尺竿頭不動人) ('the person unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole', 8 / 8).

First line here reads (不動人) ('the unmoving person').

Occurrences.Kwic: 百尺竿頭須進步，十方世界是全身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集) (Zutang ji, the Patriarchs' Hall Collection, c. 952 — TEI title 祖堂集; NOT 中峰廣錄, Zhongfeng's extensive record, and 中峰/中峯 does not occur in this file). The verse sits under Changsha's OWN governing mulu head (岑和尚) (岑和尚嗣南泉, 'Master Cen, heir of Nanquan') and is introduced (師當時有偈曰) ('the master then had a gāthā'), i.e. it is Changsha Jingcen's own verse — the earliest witness here, predating the (五燈會元) (Compendium of the Five Lamps). Immediately followed by (三聖) (Sansheng Huiran) questioning it (承師有言『百尺竿頭須進步』, 'I have it that you, master, said: atop the hundred-foot pole one must step forward'). MasterName = Changsha Jingcen (his own verse, per the governing head).
